backups.name: South Ridge
backups.season: Jul-Sep (best); snow lingers in the gully into Aug
hazards: Loose, crumbly phyllite/greenstone rock throughout the gully and upper ridge — frequent rockfall
Steep, often corniced snow-filled summit gully lingers into July
Easy to mistakenly follow a boot path toward the East Ridge instead of the correct South/SW line
backups.overview: A striking reddish peak in the Border Peaks group of the Mount Baker Wilderness, 1.4 miles south of the Canada–US border and immediately southeast of taller American Border Peak. The rust color comes from oxidized iron in the peak's phyllite and greenstone rock. First climbed September 11, 1908 by James J. McArthur's party, it's now one of the most popular scrambles near Mount Baker, typically done from a Twin Lakes camp and often paired with American Border Peak.
backups.beta: From High Pass, descend into the basin below the peak. Traverse west and ascend boulder fields and scree to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 feet. Locate the gully system in the rocky face with two narrow channels 30 feet apart; take the right channel and ascend the narrow then open gully to broken rock to attain the ridge top. Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the summit. Most of ridge top has a way trail and the route is partially marked with cairns after leaving the basin, but cairns may be far apart and the way trail may disappear for long stretches. If you lose cairns or way trail most gullies probably work though some may be more difficult than others.
backups.turnaround: Turn around well before dark to ensure safe descent. If summit is not reached by early afternoon, consider turning around to allow sufficient daylight for safe descent. The approach trail can be difficult to locate in poor visibility or darkness.
backups.rappels: None required - the descent reverses the ascent line as a walk-off/downclimb. There are no fixed rappel anchors on the route.
backups.face: South/Southwest side — crosses the South Ridge onto the SW-face gully
backups.permit: No wilderness permit required; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell phone reception is unreliable in the area and should not be counted on for emergencies. Satellite communicators (like Garmin InReach or SPOT) are strongly recommended for parties venturing into this remote alpine terrain.
obj_haz: Loose, rotten phyllite/greenstone rock in the summit gully and ridge
Rockfall onto climbers below in the gully
Persistent steep snowfields between Low Pass and High Pass into midsummer
Avalanche terrain on the approach in early season
Cornices on the north side of the summit ridge
Black bear activity along the High Pass approach

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee kiosk at the road end beside Twin Lakes; the last ~2 miles of FS-3065 below it are rough and need a high-clearance vehicle.
waypoints.directions: Drive Twin Lakes Road (FS 3065) past the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and up the final, roughly two-mile rough section to the road end at Twin Lakes, where a Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee is needed. The road is snow-gated through winter and spring. That last section is steep and rutted and needs a high-clearance vehicle, so many parties park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and walk it.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp at the alpine lake basin between Winchester and Bear Mountains; last reliable water before the high traverse to Low and High Passes.
waypoints.directions: The lakes lie at the road end, in the basin between Winchester and Bear Mountains. Fill water here. These lakes are the last reliable source before the high traverse to Low and High Passes, and there is nothing dependable past High Pass in late season.

waypoints.name: Low Pass
waypoints.note: Trail contours Winchester Mountain's east shoulder and drops through Low Pass before climbing again toward High Pass; boot path is easy to lose here in fog or lingering snow.
waypoints.directions: From the lakes follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) about half a mile to a signed junction. The left branch climbs to the Winchester lookout, so take the right fork onto the High Pass Trail (#676). It runs through meadows across Winchester Mountain's east shoulder and crosses an avalanche chute where steep, exposed snow can hang on into August, then reaches the notch of Low Pass. Carry an ice axe and know how to use it while that chute still holds snow, and expect to lose the boot path through the pass itself in fog or lingering snow.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: Basin-facing pass with the first close views of Larrabee's south face; leave the maintained High Pass Trail here and traverse cross-country toward the peak.
waypoints.directions: Climb again out of Low Pass on the High Pass Trail, a little over half a mile and about 300 feet of gain, passing the tailings and ruins of the old Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is a scenic but wind-exposed spot with the first close look at Larrabee's south face. It is also the end of the maintained trail.

waypoints.name: South Ridge crossing / SW Face gullies
waypoints.note: Boot up ~40-degree scree/snow slopes to cross the south ridge onto the southwest-face gully system; Larrabee's rock is notoriously loose and crumbly, so a helmet is essential.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the unmarked climbers' path as it contours and drops 100 to 200 feet northwest into the basin under Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band near 6,400 feet. Cross boulder fields and then scree and dirt, booting up steep ground to the southwest spur at about 6,900 feet. Cairns mark parts of this but they sit far apart and the way trail vanishes for long stretches, and boot paths here can pull you toward the East Ridge, so hold to the south and southwest side of the peak.

waypoints.name: Mount Larrabee Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,865 ft), 1.4 mi south of the Canada–US border; descend by reversing the south ridge/gully system back through the scree basin to High Pass.
waypoints.directions: From the spur, find the gully system cut into the rock face: two narrow parallel channels about thirty feet apart, of which the right-hand one is the line. It starts tight and opens into broken rock, Class 3 to 4 on loose phyllite, and holds steep snow into July and sometimes August. Climb it one person at a time with helmets on, since anything knocked loose runs straight down onto whoever is below. It tops out on the crest of the south ridge; follow the crest to the summit, favoring the west side and the firmer rock of the rib over the gully floor, with a faint way trail and scattered cairns coming and going.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Twin Lakes trailhead, follow the High Pass trail north over Low Pass and High Pass, then leave the trail a short way past High Pass and traverse/descend slightly into the basin below…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Twin Lakes to summit and back, car-to-car

backups.detailed_rack: No technical gear required; a few pieces optional for confidence on the steeper steps.
what_to_bring: Climbing helmet (essential — the rock is notoriously loose)
Ice axe and crampons/microspikes for early-season snow (through roughly July)
Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking
Trekking poles for the scree/talus sections
pro_tips: Climb the summit gully one person at a time — dislodged rock is a serious hazard to anyone below
Favor the rib/ridge crest over the gully itself, especially on descent, for firmer footing
Stay on the South/SW line; parties have mistakenly followed a boot path toward the East Ridge
Often combined with neighboring American Border Peak from the same Twin Lakes camp
watch_out: Rockfall in the gully — climb one at a time and wear a helmet
Snow and ice in the gully can persist into July; carry an ice axe and crampons/microspikes for early-season trips
Don't follow the boot path toward the East Ridge by mistake
backups.best_season: August–September for the driest, most solid conditions; late-June/early-July ascents are feasible but require ice axe and crampons/microspikes for a steep snow gully.
backups.approach: Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065 (the last 2 miles are rough, high-clearance terrain — many parties park lower and walk the road). From the trailhead, follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) briefly; at about 0.5 mile a signed junction splits left to Winchester Lookout and right onto the High Pass Trail (#676) — take the right fork. High Pass Trail #676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain (steep, exposed snowfields can linger here into August — an ice axe and snow-travel experience are recommended until the chute melts out), then continues up over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the old tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is reached roughly 2 miles / 1.5–2 hours from the trailhead and makes a scenic, if exposed, campsite. There is no reliable water past this point in late season, so treat/carry water from Twin Lakes or early snowmelt. Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends; an unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100–200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face (around 6,400 ft you pass a small cliff band). Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 ft. Here the route-finding crux: locate a gully system cut into the rock face — of two narrow parallel channels about 30 feet apart, take the RIGHT-hand one. Ascend the narrowing gully, which opens into broken rock, to gain the crest of the south ridge. Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit; a faint boot path and scattered cairns mark much of this stretch but both disappear for long sections, so be prepared to route-find. Total distance is roughly 8–10 miles round trip with on the order of 3,500–4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain (the up-and-over via Low Pass and High Pass adds real gain beyond straight-line distance to the summit). The rock throughout — especially the gully and upper ridge — is notoriously loose and crumbly by Cascades standards; helmets are strongly recommended and parties should keep group size small (6 or fewer) and spread out to manage rockfall risk to those below.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no technical descent gear needed and this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, follow the ridge crest (favoring the west side) back down to where you gained it, then descend the gully system, taking the same right-hand channel used on the way up; this loose, narrow gully is the most hazard-prone part of the descent (parties frequently trigger rockfall here even while descending carefully — down-climb one at a time or spread well apart, and keep helmets on). Below the gully, cross the broken rock and scree back down to the southwest spur (~6,900 ft) and continue down through the boulder fields and basin to regain the climbers' path near High Pass, watching for the intermittent cairns since the way trail vanishes in spots. From High Pass, retrace the High Pass Trail (#676) back over Low Pass, across the avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain (glissading or plunge-stepping lingering snow here can save time in early/mid season, but stay alert to runout hazard), and down the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) to the Twin Lakes Trailhead.
backups.bail: No fixed rappel anchors; bailing means downclimbing the same ridge/gully back to High Pass. Wet rock or a whiteout on the upper mountain significantly raises rockfall and route-finding risk, so turn around early if weather closes in.

pitch_detail.notes: Maintained High Pass Trail via Low Pass then High Pass, roughly 2.3 miles one-way; can hold snow/avalanche debris into summer.
Leave the trail a short way past High Pass, traverse/descend about 100-200 ft into the basin, then ascend boulder fields, scree, and dirt to the southwest spur near 6,900 ft.
pitch_detail.pitch: High Pass basin to SW spur

pitch_detail.notes: Two narrow gully channels about 30 ft apart split the rocky face; take the right-hand one, ascending narrow then open gully through loose, broken rock to the ridge crest.
Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit.

itinerary.cal: Twin Lakes Rd (FS 3065) can be rough or seasonally gated below the lakes, and the gully often holds snow into July, favoring an ice axe/microspikes for early-season attempts.

days.note: From the Twin Lakes trailhead, follow the High Pass trail north over Low Pass and High Pass, then leave the trail a short way past High Pass and traverse/descend slightly into the basin below Larrabee's south face. Scramble scree and boulders to a gully system at ~6,900 ft (take the right-hand of two narrow chutes), climb loose rock to gain the south ridge, then follow the ridge crest (favoring the west side) to the summit. Descend by reversing the route — the loose, chossy rock makes the descent nearly as slow as the ascent, and a helmet is considered mandatory due to rockfall.
days.title: Twin Lakes to summit and back, car-to-car

schedule.label: Leave trailhead area
schedule.detail: Twin Lakes Rd is rough/rutted and sometimes gated below the lakes; if impassable, park near Yellow Aster Butte TH, adding ~2.3 mi each way and ~1,500 ft of climbing on the walk in.

schedule.label: Twin Lakes, start High Pass trail
schedule.detail: Head north past the lakes toward Low Pass then High Pass.

schedule.label: Leave trail, enter south-face basin
schedule.detail: A short way past High Pass, traverse and drop slightly into the basin facing Larrabee's south side.

schedule.label: Ascend the gully
schedule.detail: At ~6,900 ft find the two narrow parallel chutes; take the right-hand one, staying climber's right on better rock, to broken terrain and the ridge crest.

schedule.label: Summit (7,865 ft)
schedule.detail: Follow the ridge, favoring the west side, to the top.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Reverse the full route; loose rock makes downclimbing the gully slow and rockfall-prone.

days.objective: Summit Mount Larrabee via the South Ridge gully

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: roughly 8 miles round trip with about 4,200 ft of gain, typically 7-9 hours including a slow, loose descent; strong parties have done it in 6, casual parties closer to 9-10.

access.rules: Leave No Trace; Mount Baker Wilderness regulations apply (group size limited to 12, no campfires, foot travel only)
access.permit: None for day use; wilderness practices
access.closures: Twin Lakes Road rough and snow-gated seasonally
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.

overnight_permit.where: A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at the trailhead; camp on snow, rock or bare ground at the designated tarns/sites and pack out human waste.

road.name: Twin Lakes Road (FS Road 3065)
road.status: Rough high-clearance road near the top
road.driveNote: High clearance is recommended for the final ~2 miles beyond the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead; per the Forest Service, 4WD helps but isn't strictly required, and many parties park early and walk in.

climate.typical: Snow lingers on the upper mountain into July; the summit gully is often a steep snow chute requiring ice axe/crampons through late June–early July, transitioning to a dry, loose-rock scramble by August. First snow can return by late September–October.

bySeason.fall: Late September–October: first snow possible and shorter days, but still climbable in good weather.
bySeason.spring: Generally not climbed — Twin Lakes Road is usually still snowed-in or impassable.
bySeason.summer: August–September: typically dry loose talus/scree and rock scramble; the most reliable window.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — road access is closed by snow.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North / Mount Baker area (daily avalanche forecasts run roughly Thanksgiving–April; use the general Mountain Weather Forecast for summer trip planning).

emergency.notes: No cell coverage at Twin Lakes, Low Pass, or High Pass — plan accordingly and consider a satellite communicator.
emergency.rangerStation: Glacier Public Service Center (Mt. Baker Ranger District), 10091 Mt. Baker Hwy, Glacier, WA — (360) 599-2714
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth St. Joseph Medical Center, 2901 Squalicum Pkwy, Bellingham, WA — (360) 734-5400
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Whatcom County Sheriff's Office non-emergency (360) 676-6911; dial 911 for emergencies. Search and rescue is coordinated through the Sheriff's Office via Whatcom County Search & Rescue (Bellingham Mountain Rescue unit).

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in late July and August during the short dry window
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Likely 20-40 parties per season attempt the South Ridge; the Twin Lakes/Yellow Aster Butte trailhead itself is heavily used (lots are reportedly full by 9am on weekends), but most of that hiking traffic peels off before the scramble begins

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strenuous full day; roughly 8 miles and significant elevation gain if done car-to-car, or a shorter summit push if camped at Twin Lakes
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack for the summit push; overnight pack if establishing the Twin Lakes camp described in the beta

partner_requirements.approachTime: ~2-3 hrs hiking in to Twin Lakes/High Pass area for a day trip; multi-day parties hike in and camp at Twin Lakes first, then face a shorter (~6 hr) summit day
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling on loose, blocky rock
Route-finding on ridge and gully terrain (staying on the more solid rib, avoiding the looser gully)
Rockfall awareness and helmet use - small party size recommended to reduce rockfall risk to others
Basic snow travel/kick-stepping for lingering early-season snow near the ridge
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate to advanced scrambler; prior Class 3-4 scrambling experience strongly recommended given sustained loose rock and summit exposure

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with late July-August as the most reliable stretch

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow patches; conditions firm up and become optimal by late month

June.reason: Still snow-covered and Twin Lakes Road is often gated/impassable this early

August.reason: Best window - dry rock, road open, most stable weather

September.reason: Still within the best-season; cooler and more stable, but shorter daylight for the full day

weather.typical: Wet maritime climate typical of the North Cascades border peaks, with only brief stable windows in summer
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving weather can develop in July-August; check forecasts before committing to the exposed upper ridge

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained Class 3-4 exposure with real fall consequence near the summit; the loose rock, rockfall, and summit exposure hazards are compounded by climbers above/below on the same rib, which is why trip reports recommend small parties (6 or fewer) and helmets

avalanche.zone: Mount Baker zone (NWAC) covers this part of the North Cascades border region, though it is a general-area forecast rather than a Larrabee-specific product

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on the South Ridge

gaps: Exact current Northwest Forest Pass fee amount not confirmed

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes, High Pass Trail #676 over Low Pass, then the basin to the southwest spur
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065; the last two miles are rough and many parties park lower and walk the road. From the trailhead follow Winchester Mountain Trail #685 briefly; at about half a mile a signed junction splits LEFT to the Winchester lookout and RIGHT onto High Pass Trail #676. Take the right fork.

#676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain, where steep exposed snowfields can linger into August, then goes over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is roughly two miles and an hour and a half to two hours from the trailhead. There is no reliable water past this point late season.

Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends. An unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100-200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at about 6,900 ft.

Keep the party to six or fewer and spread out. The rock here is notoriously loose even by Cascades standards.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep at best; snow lingers in the gully into August and in the avalanche chute below Winchester
hazards: Two nearly identical parallel gullies thirty feet apart, only one of which is the route
Notoriously loose and crumbly rock in the gully and on the upper ridge — helmets, small parties, spread out
An avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain holding steep snow into August
A faint boot path and cairns that disappear for long sections above the gully
No reliable water past High Pass late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO NARROW PARALLEL CHANNELS ABOUT THIRTY FEET APART. TAKE THE RIGHT-HAND ONE. That is the route-finding crux of the whole climb, it is at the southwest spur around 6,900 ft, and it is the sentence to have memorised before you leave camp. Both channels are cut into the same rock face, both look plausible, and only one of them opens into broken rock and gains the south ridge cleanly.

FINDING THE SPUR ITSELF, in order and without needing a view: leave the maintained trail at High Pass. Contour WEST on the climbers' path and lose 100-200 ft into the basin. Pass a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, and climb to about 6,900 ft. Losing height first is counterintuitive and correct; a party that only ever goes up from High Pass ends up on Larrabee's south arm ridge instead of in the basin under its face.

CONFIRM THE GULLY BY WHAT IT DOES: the right-hand channel NARROWS and then opens into broken rock that leads to the crest of the south ridge. A channel that stays uniform, or that cliffs out, is the other one.

ABOVE THE GULLY, FAVOUR THE WEST SIDE OF THE CREST. There is a faint boot path and scattered cairns, and both disappear for long stretches, so this is genuine route-finding rather than following.

WHAT THE NEIGHBOURING OBJECTIVE LOOKS LIKE: from the same High Pass the col in Larrabee's SOUTH ARM leads northeast to the Pleiades and the traverse under Larrabee's west flank leads to American Border Peak. Three separate objectives leave from one pass, so name yours before you set off.

climbing_route.label: Right-hand gully from the southwest spur
climbing_route.notes: From the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 ft, the route-finding crux: locate a gully system cut into the rock face and, of two narrow parallel channels about 30 feet apart, take the RIGHT-hand one. Ascend the narrowing gully, which opens into broken rock, to gain the crest of the south ridge. The rock here is notoriously loose and crumbly by Cascades standards; helmets are strongly recommended and parties should keep group size small (6 or fewer) and spread out to manage rockfall risk to those below.

climbing_route.label: South ridge crest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit. A faint boot path and scattered cairns mark much of this stretch but both disappear for long sections, so be prepared to route-find. The upper ridge rock is loose and crumbly.

bivy.name: High Pass camp
bivy.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
bivy.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
bivy.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

bivy.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
bivy.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pack costs you nothing, so most parties on Winchester, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak sleep here and start from the isthmus between the lakes. The Winchester Mountain trail and the High Pass trail both begin there. It does not melt out completely until July in most years, and late-season parties should expect a busy, social camp rather than a quiet one. Everything the lakes hold is heavily used; pick an established site rather than making a new one in the meadow.
bivy.water: The two lakes, right at camp. No treated water; filter or boil.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
bivy.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend

bivy.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
bivy.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
bivy.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower

backups.name: Cougar Divide Route
hazards: Loose rock and talus on the final Class 2/3 scramble to the summit.
Steep, loose terrain along sections of the ridge traverse with a drop-off to one side.
Snow on the ridge can persist into early summer, requiring an ice axe and creating slip hazard on the traverse.
backups.overview: A shorter, higher-starting alternative to the Skyline Divide approach, climbing the Cougar Divide ridge trail from the end of FS Road 33 to Chowder Ridge before joining the same Class 2 scramble to Hadley Peak's summit.
backups.beta: From the Cougar Divide Trailhead (~4,900 ft), the unmaintained Cougar Divide Trail #601 climbs along a ridge crest through meadows and old growth to its high point near 5,920 ft (about 3.1 miles in). From there the route continues cross-country along the open ridge, crossing toward Dobbs Cleaver/Chowder Ridge, to merge with the Skyline Divide approach below Hadley Peak's northwest ridge. The final push to the summit is Class 2 with a brief Class 3 step over loose scree, with generally mild exposure for experienced scramblers.
backups.turnaround: Set a turnaround time that allows a full daylight margin for the return along the ridge and loose summit scramble, and avoid the final scramble block in wet or icy conditions given the loose rock underfoot.
backups.face: Northwest Ridge (Chowder Ridge - Hadley Peak connecting ridge)
backups.permit: Free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell coverage is unreliable in this area; no dependable service should be expected on the drive in or along the ridge — carry a satellite communicator for emergencies.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose summit scramble, retrace the ridge back to the Cougar Divide Trail high point, and follow the trail back to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Cougar Divide Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of NF Road 33 off Mount Baker Highway (SR-542); road closed Nov 1–Jul 7 for wildlife protection. Higher/shorter start than Skyline Divide.

backups.detailed_rack: None — this is a non-technical class 2-3 scramble with no roped climbing; no rack, rope, or protection is used.
what_to_bring: Recreation/day-use pass or annual Interagency pass for the trailhead
self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box
pro_tips: Cougar Divide's trailhead sits notably higher (~4,900 ft) than Skyline Divide's, making this the shorter and less-crowded of the two standard approaches.
FS Road 33 is gated seasonally (closed roughly Nov 1-Jul 7 for wildlife protection) — confirm the gate is open before driving out.
The actual trailhead is reported to be roughly a kilometer beyond where mapping apps typically route drivers along FS 33 — don't stop early.
watch_out: FS Road 33 is closed to vehicles annually from November 1 through July 7 to protect wildlife; the route is not accessible by this approach outside that window.
Loose rock and a steep dropoff to one side along parts of the ridge traverse.
Severe mosquitoes are commonly reported until mid-summer on the meadow sections.
backups.pro_needs: No fixed protection or rope is used on the standard scramble line; an ice axe is the main security item carried, useful for residual snow on the ridge in early or late season.
backups.best_season: The higher Cougar Divide trailhead (~4,900 ft, versus Skyline Divide's lower start) makes this a shorter outing once the seasonal road gate opens; ideal timing is roughly mid-August through early October, avoiding early-season mosquitoes and late-season snow on the ridge.
backups.approach: From Glacier, WA, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east and turn onto Forest Service Road 33; follow roughly 11 miles of gravel road (rough in sections, high-clearance/SUV recommended, sedans passable with care) to its end at the Cougar Divide Trailhead/parking (room for 8-10 vehicles). Note the true trailhead may be roughly another kilometer past where online mapping apps route. Hike Cougar Divide Trail #601 along the ridge to its high point (~5,920 ft), then continue cross-country south along the open ridge, crossing near Dobbs Creek, to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley Peak's final scramble.
backups.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb the short Class 3 step and loose scree back onto the connecting ridge, then retrace the cross-country ridge traverse back to the Cougar Divide Trail's high point (~5,920 ft). Follow the unmaintained Cougar Divide Trail #601 back down through meadows and forest to the trailhead.
backups.bail: The route can be abandoned at any point by retracing the ridge crest and Cougar Divide Trail back to the trailhead; no fixed rappel or technical retreat is required.

approach_variants.name: Cougar Divide Trail #601 and the open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east and turn onto Forest Service Road 33; follow about 11 miles of gravel — rough in sections, high-clearance recommended, sedans passable with care — to its end at the Cougar Divide trailhead, with room for eight to ten vehicles. The true trailhead may be roughly a kilometre past where online mapping routes you, so do not stop at the first turnaround that looks right.

Hike Cougar Divide Trail #601 along the ridge to its high point around 5,920 ft. That high point is where the trail tread ends and the route becomes cross-country: continue south along the open ridge, crossing near Dobbs Creek, to Chowder Ridge and the foot of Hadley's summit block.

This and the Skyline Divide route are two different walks to the SAME summit block; the beta below for the block is common to both.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct, once the ridge is out from under snow
hazards: Eleven miles of rough gravel road, and a trailhead that mapping apps place short of the real one
Cross-country ridge travel with no tread and no cairns once past the 5,920 ft high point
Loose scree below a short Class 3 step
Open ridge with no shelter and no water beyond the trailhead
In cloud, two different divides converge on this summit and neither exit is marked
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RIDGE IS THE ROUTE AND ITS HIGH POINT IS THE HANDOFF. Trail #601 runs along the crest to a high point near 5,920 ft, and everything after that is open ridge. In cloud you do not need a view: stay on the crest, going south, with the ground falling away on both sides. The moment you are sidehilling with the drop on only one side, you have come off the divide.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING, and this is the test that matters: the summit block of Hadley is a SHORT CLASS 3 STEP above loose scree, roughly the last 100 ft of the day. Everything below it is walking. So the base is the point where the ridge stops being walkable and stands up in a single short step. If you are scrambling for hundreds of feet you are on the wrong feature; if you have not scrambled at all you are not at the summit.

THE APPROACH IS NOT A LOOP AND CHOWDER RIDGE IS THE CONFIRMATION. You should arrive at the block having travelled along Chowder Ridge. If you are dropping into a basin or crossing a glacier to reach a rock block, you are somewhere else on the north side of Baker.

WHICH DIVIDE DID YOU WALK IN ON? This is the one thing to be sure of before you commit to a descent line in poor visibility, because the two approaches to this summit leave in different directions and neither is signed. Cougar Divide comes in from the NORTH, straight down its own ridge; Skyline Divide comes in from the WEST, a parallel ridge about a mile and a half over across the Deadhorse Creek valley, and is the much longer walk. Note your entry point onto Chowder Ridge on the way up.

bivy.name: Cougar Divide meadow camps
bivy.notes: This is the north-side approach to Hadley Peak and it has nothing to do with the Black Buttes or the Coleman — a party here is on the far side of the mountain from the Heliotrope Ridge climbers. Cougar Divide is an unofficial, unmaintained path along the ridge crest, reached from Wells Creek Road, whose first several miles are badly potholed to the Nooksack bridge and then improve. From the meadows at the head of the divide the ground opens onto Chowder Ridge, and the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley. The gate opening in July combined with mosquitoes that are genuinely bad here until midsummer pushes the sensible window to mid-August through early October, which is also when the talus is clear and the route is straightforward walking with the odd second-class step.
bivy.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

bivy.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
bivy.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.
bivy.water: The most reliable water on the Hadley approach — the creek runs from snowmelt above the basin and holds up later than anything on the ridge crests. Treat it. This is the reason to camp here rather than higher.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

gear: Quickdraws — the route is fully bolted up the lichen-covered basalt band on Pinto Rock's north face; bring a standard sport rack for the pitch length rather than a trad rack
60m rope — single rope is fine; descent is two rappels down the route from its own chain anchors
Helmet — basalt is knobby and generally solid, but loose blocks and other parties above are a real concern on this face
Alpine quickdraws/slings for rigging the rappels at the chain anchors
hazards: Remote, multi-mile forest-road approach from the nearest town

Two-pitch sport climbing requires rappel competency, unlike most single-pitch lines at this crag
backups.overview: A two-pitch bolted line up the left (west) side of Pinto Rock's north-facing basalt band, with an easy warm-up pitch leading to a harder roof-pull finish.
backups.beta: P1 (5.5) climbs about 100 ft up slabby rock on 7 bolts to a chain anchor; P2 (5.10c/d) continues about 80 ft on 9 bolts through the route's crux, pulling a roof near the top. Rated 5.10b overall. It shares the same lichen-covered basalt band as Sidewinder but follows it up and to the left rather than traversing right.
backups.turnaround: No fixed turnaround time is documented; as with any two-pitch sport route here, start early enough to finish both rappels and hike out before dark given the steep, loose descent trail.
backups.rappels: Rappel the route (chain anchors at each pitch)
